A novel lightweight multi-scale 
feature fusion segmentation 
algorithm for real-time cervical 
lesion screening
Jiahui Yang1, Ying Zhang1, Wenlong Fan1, Jie Wang1, Xinhe Zhang1, Chunhui Liu2, 
Shuang Liu1,3,4 & Linyan Xue1,3,4
AI-based cervical lesion segmentation in colposcopy images has significant potential in improving 
screening efficiency and accuracy. However, most current cervical lesion segmentation algorithms are 
insufficient for rapid image segmentation in mass screening due to heavy parameters and complex 
framework. Therefore, a lightweight algorithm segmentation for cervical lesion real-time screening 
system is urgently needed. In this paper, a novel lightweight LSIL + region segmentation framework 
termed Light-MDDNet is proposed and deployed, which uses the encoder-decoder architecture. In 
encoder stage, the first layer of MobileNetV2 module outputs shallow features which tend to be lost 
during multi-layer feature extraction. We also utilize the Denseaspp module to extract deeper semantic 
information. In the decoder stage, a multi-scale feature fusion (MFF) module is used to fuse multi-
scale features. Finally, the algorithm is deployed and tested on the JETSON ORIN NX edge device in 
cervical lesion segmentation screening system. The experiments on 971 LSIL + colposcopy images of 
lesions processed with acetic acid show that our proposed model outperforms some state-of-the-art 
segmentation networks, with a pixel mean pixel accuracy (MPA) of 94.96% and an average speed per 
image of 19.60ms. After deployment on the mobile terminal, the segmentation accuracy of the model 
almost unchanged and the interference speed reduces to 31.57ms per image. The Light-MDDNet 
network achieves the best balance of accuracy and speed in cervical lesion segmentation, showing 
great potential for the deployment in the mass screening of cervical lesion.
Keywords  Colposcopy images, Image segmentation, Deep learning, Lightweight
Cervical cancer ranks fourth among new cases and deaths of cancer in women worldwide, accounting for 6.5% 
and 7.7% of total incidence and mortality, respectively1. The early cure rate of cervical cancer can reach over 95%, 
while the late cure rate drops to 20–50%2–6. Although cervical cancer is one of the most preventable cancers, it 
still ranks second among cancer deaths in women aged 20 to 39, mainly due to difficulty in diagnosis caused by 
the lack of obvious symptoms in the early stage7. In recent years, the AI-based cervical lesion segmentation to 
colposcopy assisted diagnostic system helps to observe the condition of the lesion and plays an important role 
in cervical cancer pre-screening8.
The research on cervical lesion segmentation in colposcopy images generally focus on the segmentation of 
low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesions or worse (LSIL+) areas to assist doctors in improving diagnostic 
efficiency and accuracy9. Praba et al.10 proposed a fully automatic lesion detection method based on color 
histograms, which removes irrelevant information and mirror reflections through preprocessing, then 
extracts color histogram features, and uses KNN, naïve Bayes, and SVM classifiers to detect lesion area, with 
a segmentation accuracy of over 85%. Liu et al.11 used the k-means clustering algorithm to extract the cervical 
region and the DeepLab V3 + image semantic segmentation model based on deep learning to segment the Lesion 
area, with an average accuracy of 91.2%. Yue et al.12 designed a mirror reflection removal method, proposing

the AWL-CNN network with 90.6% accuracy. Yuan et al.13 used ResNet to replace the encoding part of U-Net 
to segment LSIL + areas, achieving a 95.59% average accuracy for acetic images. Yu et al.14 proposed the CLS-
Model for segmenting LSIL + areas in post-acetic cervical lesion images under colposcopy, with 93.04% accuracy. 
However, most current cervical lesion segmentation algorithms cannot be effectively adopted for rapid image 
segmentation in the mass screening of cervical lesion as they are parameter-heavy, computationally complex 
and slow to use.
The application of lightweight networks in medical image segmentation is becoming increasingly 
widespread, as they can improve segmentation efficiency and effectively utilize computing resources. Jeya et 
al.15 proposed UNeXt, which is an image segmentation network based on Convolutional Multilayer Perceptron 
(MLP), including the early convolution stage and the latent MLP stage, reducing the number of parameters 
by 72x, decrease the computational complexity by 68x, and improve the inference speed by 10x. Azad et al.16 
proposed a Transformer based medical image segmentation method, which improves the efficiency of medical 
image segmentation through multi-scale feature fusion. Heidari et al.17 proposed a Double-Level Fusion (DLF) 
module in the skip connection of the encoder-decoder structure. Extensive experiments on various medical 
image segmentation datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of HiFormer over other CNNbased, transformer-
based, and hybrid methods in terms of computational complexity, quantitative and qualitative results Sun et al.18 
proposed segmentation and localization of liver CT images based on Deeplabv3+, and has been proven to have 
very good performance, Lee et al.19 proposed a lightweight volumetric ConvNet, termed 3D UX-Net, which 
adapts the hierarchical transformer using ConvNet modules for robust volumetric segmentation.
This study proposes a lightweight network model and deploys it on the portable and powerful JETSON ORIN 
NX, which can achieve high-precision and real-time cervical lesion segmentation in the screening of cervical 
lesion.
The specific contributions are as follows:
	1.	 1. We propose a lightweight segmentation algorithm, Light-MDDNet, which adopts the classic framework of 
DeeplabV3+20 for cervical lesion real-time screening system.
	2.	 2. Light-MDDNet uses the encoder-decoder architecture. In encoder stage, the first layer of MobileNetV­
221module outputs shallow features, which is easily lost after multi-layer feature extraction .We also utilize 
the Denseaspp22 module to extract deeper semantic information. In the decoder stage, a multi-scale feature 
fusion (MFF) module is used to fuse multi-scale features.
	3.	 3. This paper create a high-quality cervical lesion segmentation dataset. We use Light-MDDNet to segment 
our cervical cancer segmentation dataset and achieve hardware deployment on the high-performance JET­
SON ORIN NX mobile device for the screening of cervical lesion. The experimental results show that the 
proposed network model in this paper can best balance segmentation accuracy and test speed.
Materials and methods
Overall architecture
Figure 1 shows the encoder-decoder architecture of the proposed Light-MDDNet. In encoder stage, the first 
layer of MobileNetV2 module outputs shallow features, which is easily lost after multi-layer feature extraction. 
We also utilize the Denseaspp module to extract deep features, as the lightweight MobileNetV2 is insufficient in 
representing deeper semantic information. In the decoder stage, a multi-scale feature fusion (MFF) module is 
used to fuse multi-scale features outputted by different layer of MobileNetV2.
MobileNetV2 module
MobileNetV2 is a lightweight deep learning model which introduces linear bottlenecks and inverted residual 
structures. The linear bottleneck compresses the input feature map through a 1 × 1 convolution, then performs

the Bottleneck is repeated, c is the depth channel of the output feature matrix, s represents the stride of the first 
layer in each operator.
Denseaspp
The lesion areas in colposcopy images have variable shapes and different scales. Traditional convolution or 
pooling operations cannot capture this deeper semantic information. Thus, we use DenseASPP module rather 
than ASPP module to extract more effective deep feature. The structure of DenseASPP is shown in Fig. 2.
In DenseASPP, contextual information is extracted by performing dilated convolution on multiple feature 
maps and adding a new dilated convolution after each dilated convolution. Using this method, each dilated 
convolution can extract contextual information of different scales, with this information being cumulative. In 
DenseASPP, 5 dilated layers with different dilation rates are used, which are 3,6,12,18,and 24,respectively.The

Multi-level feature fusion module
Multiple feature sizes are obtained when using MobileNetV2 to extract features from colposcopy images. Low-
level features contain more position and detail information, but their semantics are lower and there is more 
noise. High-level features have stronger semantic information, but their ability to perceive details is poor. We 
use the MFF module to fuse feature maps of different scales outputted by MobileNetV2 module, the detailed 
structure is shown in Fig. 3.

Transfer learning
In the realm of computer vision, the concept of transfer learning24 is frequently utilized, particularly in the 
context of representing pre-trained models. These models consist of weights and biases that have been previously 
trained on extensive benchmark datasets. These parameters are fine-tuned through the backpropagation 
algorithm, using substantial training datasets. As a result, pre-trained models are adept at discerning general

features and patterns, which can be effectively applied to a variety of tasks.
Addressing the challenge of limited training data in the domain of colposcopy image segmentation, transfer 
learning was employed in backbone networks of our Light-MDDNet and other comparative networks. These 
include VGG25, ResNet5026, MobileNet27, Xception28, Swin-T29and Swin-B29. Each of these networks has been 
augmented with pre-trained weights derived from training on the VOC12 + SBD dataset. This integration 
leverages the power of transfer learning to enhance the performance of our models in tasks with constrained 
data availability.

Experiment
Data Collection and Preparation
A total of 971 images from 971 patients taken by colposcope at the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University 
between June 2019 and February 2023 were analyzed. The images were of pathological cervical lesions processed 
with acetic acid. Gynecologic oncologists annotated the images according to pathological lesions (see Fig. 4).
Experiment
Data Collection and Preparation
The dataset used in this study comprises 971 cervical images collected from 971 patients using a colposcope 
at the Affiliated Hospital of Hebei University between June 2019 and February 2023. These images, taken after 
acetic acid processing to highlight pathological cervical lesions, were meticulously annotated by gynecologic 
oncologists based on pathological lesion characteristics. An example of an annotated image is presented in Fig. 4.
In addition to this dataset, we conducted cross-dataset validation using an independent dataset collected 
from the same hospital during a subsequent phase. This secondary dataset, gathered from February 2023 to 
June 2024, includes 197 cervical images from 197 patients. Crucially, these images were not involved in model 
training, ensuring an unbiased evaluation of the model’s generalization ability.
Training strategy
We use a machine with one NVIDIA GTX 2080Ti GPU for model training. We randomly split the vaginal 
endoscopy dataset into training and test sets in a 9:1 ratio. The loss function used for network training is 
cross entropy. We utilize the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) optimizer to train our network, setting the 
momentum at 0.9, the weight decay at 0.0001 and the initial learning rate of 0.01. To ensure the fairness of 
the experiments, all methods are trained on the same training data and transfer learning was employed in all 
models for the extensive data requirements associated with image segmentation tasks. The independent dataset 
of 197 images was exclusively reserved for cross-dataset validation, further substantiating the robustness and 
generalization capacity of our proposed model.

Model Deployment
In this study, we developed a workflow for deploying the Light-MDDNet for the screening of cervical lesion, 
which is depicted in the provided diagram. The process begins with the collection of images, which are then 
used to train a deep learning model on a dedicated server. Post-training, the model’s parameters are frozen. 
The trained model is then converted into an ONNX format, a step that facilitates deployment across diverse 
environments. The ONNX model undergoes further conversion to a Plan File, which is subsequently optimized 
within the PyTorch Inference Engine for efficient performance. We utilize original vaginal endoscopy images 
as input signals, feeding them into the deployed Light-MDDNet network on the JETSON ORIN NX mobile 
platform for real-time segmentation inference. Ultimately, the segmentation results are promptly displayed on a 
monitor connected via the HDMI interface, providing convenient reference and screening evidence for medical 
professionals. Figure 5 presents the overall real-time segmentation flowchart.
As shown in Table 2, the JETSON ORIN NX has higher performance than other mobile development boards 
in real-time segmentation and detection of cervical lesions. In particular, the processor’s computing power is 
much higher than other devices, reaching 100TOPS, and it has good GPU performance. At the same time, 
this device also comes with a 2 x NVDLA v2 deep learning accelerator, which can greatly improve computing 
speed, achieve real-time segmentation of cervical lesions, and meet the current needs of large-scale colposcopy 
screening work.

Results and discussion
Comparison of different segmentation networks
We compare our model with five classic image semantic segmentation models: U-Net, DeepLabV3+, HRNet, 
PSPNet, and UperNet. These algorithms use different backbone feature extraction networks, with nine 
experimental indicators used to evaluate segmentation performance when conducting the comparison. To 
ensure the fairness of the experiments, all models use the dataset constructed in this study and are trained under 
the same environment and parameter settings.
Table 3 lists the MIoU, PA, MPA, Pre, Re, and the F1 Score to measure the segmentation performance of the 
different method/backbone pairs. Our novel Light-MDDNet model is exhibited at the forefront, achieving or 
approaching the apex scores across these performance metrics. In Table 4, we present a detailed comparison 
of various methods and backbone architectures based on key metrics such as FLOPs, Params, FPS, Weight and 
Time. These metrics allow us to thoroughly evaluate the efficiency of different networks. Our findings reaffirm 
the remarkable capabilities of our network. Notably, it significantly outperforms PSPNet/ResNet50, which is the 
only competitor that comes close to our segmentation performance. Interestingly, other lightweight networks 
exhibit comparatively poor segmentation results. The success of our approach lies in its ability to achieve superior 
accuracy without relying on high internal resolution or computationally expensive convolutions. Instead, we 
emphasize the importance of a powerful multi-level feature fusion network. By extending the conventional

To further validate the generalization ability of our model, we conducted cross-dataset validation using an 
independent dataset comprising 197 patients, which was not involved in training. The experimental results, as 
presented in Table 5, demonstrate that Light-MDDNet retains outstanding segmentation performance in cross-
dataset scenarios. Specifically, Light-MDDNet achieved a MIoU of 83.23%, marking notable improvements 
compared to other methods, particularly the traditional U-Net (VGGNet and ResNet50 versions) and 
DeeplabV3+ (Xception and MobileNetV2 versions), with respective enhancements of approximately 2.49% 
and 2.35%. Moreover, Light-MDDNet also excelled in other evaluation metrics, maintaining high performance 
in MPA, Pre, Re, Dice, and Jaccard indices. Notably, Light-MDDNet demonstrated superior delineation of 
lesion boundaries, especially in challenging cases with complex backgrounds or low-contrast conditions. These 
findings underscore the robustness and adaptability of Light-MDDNet, which effectively handles variations in 
data distribution during cross-dataset testing. This highlights its potential value and broad applicability in real-
world scenarios.
Fig. 6 showcases the segmentation results for two randomly selected images, derived from eleven distinct 
segmentation methods. The ensuing Fig. 7 provides an illustrative overlay of the ground truth upon the segmented 
outcomes, employing green lines to trace the ground truth and blue lines to represent the actual segmentation 
results from multiple networks. This visual assessment demarcates the superior segmentation finesse of our 
Light-MDDNet, demonstrating its remarkable ability to generate more accurate and densely packed predictions 
that closely mirror the ground truth, outperforming its counterparts. Specifically, in the instances presented, 
the segmentation accuracy of Light-MDDNet is unparalleled, corroborating the analyses previously mentioned.
In Table 6, we provide a comparative analysis of our model, Light-MDDNet, against other cervical lesion area 
segmentation methodologies reported in the literature over the past three years. It is noteworthy that our model 
achieves exemplary performance, registering the highest PA at 94.96%. This metric is particularly significant as 
it reflects the proportion of correctly identified pixels within the lesion area, underscoring the precision of our 
model in the screening of cervical lesion.
Our model is operationalized on the JETSON ORIN NX development board, enabling high-performance

segmentation of cervical lesion areas on embedded devices. Remarkably, the model maintains an inference 
accuracy on this platform that is on par with the results obtained from our deep learning server tests. This 
consistency is achieved with an impressive average processing time of just 31.57 milliseconds per image, which 
not only attests to the model’s effectiveness but also validates its reliability and suitability for embedded systems. 
This capability is crucial for real-time applications, particularly in the screening of cervical lesion where rapid and 
accurate diagnostics are imperative. Table 7 list the segmentation performance in different testing environment.
Ablation experiment
Our ablation studies meticulously assess the contribution of individual components to the Light-MDDNet’s 
performance, with each experiment harnessing the strengths of transfer learning. The findings, as detailed 
in Table 8, reveal incremental advancements through the strategic modification of the network. Initially, the 
DeeplabV3 + network alone achieved an MIoU of 80.32%, with a processing time of 40.42 milliseconds per 
image. The integration of MobileNetV2 as the backbone significantly improved processing efficiency, reducing 
the time to 15.10 milliseconds while marginally elevating the MIoU to 81.30%. The addition of the MFF module 
further raised the MIoU to 82.13%, indicating a notable increase in segmentation accuracy with a slight increase 
in processing time. Incorporating the Denseaspp module resulted in an MIoU of 82.87%, continuing the trend of 
improved performance. Utilizing the full complement of modules, our model attained an MIoU apex of 83.94%, 
with an acceptable increment in processing time to 19.60 milliseconds. This progression not only underscores 
an enhancement in the model’s accuracy but also an uptick in processing speed, affirming that the model’s 
preeminence primarily stems from its holistic network architecture.

Conclusion
In this paper, we successfully construct a real-time auxiliary screening system to assist in the segmentation 
of cervical lesions and meet the needs of mass screening for cervical cancer. We propose Light-MDDNet, 
an innovative and compact framework designed for the segmentation of LSIL + regions, capitalizing on the 
encoder-decoder schema. The encoder employs MobileNetV2 at its inaugural layer to capture shallow features, 
which are prone to loss through successive layers of feature extraction. To mitigate this, the Denseaspp module is 
incorporated to distill deeper semantic details. During the decoding phase, the multi-scale feature fusion (MFF) 
module synergistically integrates features across different scales. Moreover, Light-MDDNet is operationalized 
on the JETSON ORIN NX platform, catering to the mass screening of cervical lesion where rapid and reliable 
processing is paramount. Our extensive experiments confirm that Light-MDDNet outperforms previous models 
in both efficiency and accuracy, demonstrating significant potential for mass screening applications and offering

considerable promise for advancements in clinical use.
Nonetheless, our study is constrained by the scarcity of publicly accessible datasets with adequate segmentation 
labels, which constrains our ability to thoroughly assess the model’s generalization capabilities.
